`kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -o name`
`kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Failed -o name` | total/phase, CrashLoop/ImagePull/OOM/restarts, images, resources, probes, SA, security, QoS, scheduling, lifecycle; describe only bounded problem samples. `kubectl get ingress -A -o json` | count/classes/annotations/status; detect controllers from bounded pod projection; Gateway API stays area 40. |\\n| 11 HPA / `HPA_JSON` | `kubectl get hpa -A -o json` | count, min/max/current, targets/conditions; autoscaling feature. |\\n| 12 VPA | `kubectl get vpa -A -o wide` | CRD-specific presence/count/mode; NotFound = feature false. |\\n| 13 KEDA | `kubectl get scaledobjects -A -o wide`

`kubectl get pv -o json`

`kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json`
`kubectl get roles -A -o json`
`kubectl get rolebindings -A -o json`
`kubectl get serviceaccounts -A -o json` | counts, wildcard/cluster-admin/non-system bindings, subjects, SA automount/IRSA metadata; never tokens. |\\n| 23 CRDS / `CRD_JSON` | `kubectl get crds -o json` | count/groups/categories only; use as hints, never as proof a specific optional API is readable. |\\n| 24 WEBHOOKS / `WEBHOOK_PROJECTION` | `kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o json`

{"id": "d76d893c-38cd-49e6-829d-7353d65dc283", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_rM3GTZIDrmW86QAYyxpxtP", "content": "[{'text': '# AWS-API & Cluster Insights checks (AX-series)\\n\\nThe fourth data source for an EKS review. The eight in-cluster pillars are graded from `kubectl`; the Control Plane Health pillar is graded from CloudWatch Logs; this component grades the facts that are **only visible from the AWS control-plane APIs and EKS Cluster Insights** \u2014 the layer that `kubectl` and CloudWatch logs cannot see.\\n\\nIt exists because a large share of real-world EKS support cases are rooted in AWS-side state that an in-cluster sweep marks `N/A`: access entries with no policy attached, nodegroups stuck in `CREATE_FAILED`, EC2 instances that launch but never register, per-subnet IP exhaustion, managed-addon upgrade conflicts, Pod Identity associations that aren\\'t active, and the AWS Load Balancer Controller\\'s IAM permissions. Cluster Insights is the authoritative AWS signal for upgrade readiness and misconfiguration. Promoting these from \"AWS-API follow-up\" to graded checks is what closes the review to full coverage.\\n\\nBest-practice anchors: [Cluster Insights](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/cluster-insights.html) \u00b7 [Cluster Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/cluster-access-management.html) \u00b7 [Managed node groups](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/managed-node-groups.html) \u00b7 [EKS add-ons](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/eks-add-ons.html) \u00b7 [Pod Identity](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/pod-identities.html) \u00b7 [VPC CNI / IP optimization](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/ip-opt.html) \u00b7 [AWS Load Balancer Controller](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/aws-load-balancer-controller.html)\\n\\n## Contents\\n\\n- Data source \u2014 read this first\\n- Official AWS API operations used\\n- How to grade\\n- Cluster Insights (AX1)\\n- Access & authentication (AX2\u2013AX3)\\n- Nodegroup & node-join health (AX4, AX8)\\n- Addon health (AX5)\\n- Workload IAM (AX6, AX9)\\n- IP & subnet capacity (AX7)\\n- Manual / config-surface checks (AX10\u2013AX14)\\n- Finding \u2192 check map (full 15-row coverage)\\n- Relationship to other pillars\\n\\n## Data source \u2014 read this first\\n\\nThis component is **not** graded from in-cluster `kubectl`. It reads the AWS control-plane APIs through the agent\\'s authorized, read-only access path (`describe*` / `list*` / `get*` on the EKS / EC2 / IAM APIs). Use read-only credentials; never a mutating call.\\n\\nGrade this component when:\\n\\n- the review scope is \"operations review\" / \"is it following best practices?\" / a CWR (grade everything), **or**\\n- the user explicitly asks about access entries, nodegroup health, addons, Pod Identity, IP exhaustion, node join failures, or load balancer controller health, **and**\\n- the agent has read access to the EKS / EC2 / IAM APIs for the cluster\\'s account.\\n\\nIf AWS-API access is unavailable, mark every check below **N/A**, state which API was unreachable, and flag it as a follow-up. Never guess an AWS-side fact.\\n\\n> **Read-only.** Every call here is a `Describe` / `List` / `Get` / policy-simulation. This component never mutates AWS resources. Remediations are drafted for human approval.\\n\\n## Official AWS API operations used\\n\\nEvery AX check maps to a documented, read-only AWS API operation (callable via `aws <service> <operation>` or any SDK). Cite the operation as the authoritative source. All EKS operations are in the [Amazon EKS API Reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/APIReference/Welcome.html).\\n\\n| Check | EKS / EC2 / IAM API operation(s) | CLI {"id": "7ddad5bd-0595-49c3-966d-e93ce9f3ceb2", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_qb3MCd3dlxixmr7uPkKzc7", "content": "[{'text': '# Security Pods Rbac remediations \u2014 shard 01\\nCanonical IDs: `S1,S2,S3,S4,S5,S6,S7,S8,S9,S10,S11,S12,S13,S14,S15`\\n\\n### S1 \u2014 No privileged containers\\n**Why it matters:** A privileged container has effectively root on the host \u2014 a container escape becomes a node compromise, then lateral movement.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Find them: `kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r \\'.items[] | .metadata as $m | .spec.containers[] | select(.securityContext.privileged==true) | \"\\\\($m.namespace)/\\\\($m.name)/\\\\(.name)\"\\'`\\n2. Remove `privileged: true`; grant only the specific Linux capability needed. Enforce with Pod Security Admission `restricted` or a policy engine.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\nsecurityContext:\\n  privileged: false\\n  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false\\n  capabilities:\\n    drop: [\"ALL\"]\\n    add: [\"NET_BIND_SERVICE\"]   # only if required\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n- [Kubernetes \u2014 Pod Security Standards](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards/)\\n\\n### S2 \u2014 No host namespaces\\n**Why it matters:** `hostNetwork`/`hostPID`/`hostIPC` break the container isolation boundary \u2014 a pod can see host processes, sniff node traffic, or share IPC with the host.\\n**Steps:** Remove host-namespace flags from workloads (legitimate only for specific system DaemonSets). Enforce via PSA `baseline`/`restricted`.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\nspec:\\n  hostNetwork: false\\n  hostPID: false\\n  hostIPC: false\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n\\n### S3 / S4 / S5 \u2014 Pod hardening (allowPrivilegeEscalation / drop ALL caps / seccomp RuntimeDefault)\\n**Why it matters:** These three together close the most common privilege-escalation and syscall-abuse paths and are exactly what the PSA `restricted` profile enforces.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Set `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, drop `ALL` capabilities, and set `seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault` on every workload container.\\n2. Enforce cluster-wide via PSA labels on namespaces or a policy engine (Kyverno/Gatekeeper) so new workloads can\\'t regress.\\n**Snippet (container + pod securityContext):**\\n```yaml\\nspec:\\n  securityContext:\\n    seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }\\n  containers:\\n    - name: ${APP}\\n      securityContext:\\n        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false\\n        runAsNonRoot: true\\n        capabilities: { drop: [\"ALL\"] }\\n```\\n**Snippet (enforce restricted on a namespace):**\\n```yaml\\nmetadata:\\n  labels:\\n    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted\\n    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Runtime Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/runtime-security.html)\\n- [Kubernetes \u2014 Enforce Pod Security Standards with Namespace Labels](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/enforce-standards-namespace-labels/)\\n\\n### S6 \u2014 readOnlyRootFilesystem\\n**Why it matters:** A writable root filesystem lets an attacker drop binaries, modify config, or persist inside a running container.\\n**Steps:** Set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`; mount `emptyDir` for the few paths the app must write (tmp, cache).\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\nsecurityContext:\\n  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true\\nvolumeMounts:\\n  - { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp }\\nvolumes:\\n  - { name: tmp, emptyDir: {} }\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n\\n### S7 \u2014 runAsNonRoot\\n**Why it matters:** Containers running as UID 0 inherit host-root capabilities on escape. Running as a non-root user is a cheap, high-value hardening.\\n**Steps:** Set `runAsNonRoot: true` (and a concrete `runAsUser`) on workloads; rebuild images with a non-root `USER` where the process requires a fixed UID.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\nsecurityContext:\\n  runAsNonRoot: true\\n  runAsUser: 1000\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n\\n### S8 \u2014 No hostPath volumes\\n**Why it matters:** A `hostPath` mount exposes the node filesystem to the pod \u2014 a path to read host secrets or escape to the node.\\n**Steps:** Replace hostPath with `emptyDir`, PVCs, or CSI volumes. Where a host mount is unavoidable (system agents), restrict to a specific path and mount read-only.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n\\n### S9 \u2014 Pod Security Admission configured\\n**Why it matters:** Without PSA labels (or a policy engine), nothing stops a workload from running privileged/root/host-namespace \u2014 the hardening checks above aren\\'t enforced, only hoped for.\\n**Steps:** Label workload namespaces with PSA `enforce`/`warn`/`audit` at `baseline` or `restricted`; or run Kyverno/Gatekeeper with equivalent policies.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\nmetadata:\\n  labels:\\n    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline\\n    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n- [Kubernetes \u2014 Enforce Pod Security Standards with Namespace Labels](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/enforce-standards-namespace-labels/)\\n\\n### S10 \u2014 No cluster-admin to non-system principals\\n**Why it matters:** A ClusterRoleBinding to `cluster-admin` for a human user, broad group, or workload SA is full cluster compromise if that identity is phished or leaked.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Find them: `kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r \\'.items[] | select(.roleRef.name==\"cluster-admin\") | \"\\\\(.metadata.name): \\\\(.subjects)\"\\'`\\n2. Replace with least-privilege roles (`view`/`edit` or custom Roles scoped to namespaces). Keep cluster-admin only for break-glass, ideally via EKS Access Entries.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Identity and Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/identity-and-access-management.html)\\n- [Kubernetes \u2014 Using RBAC Authorization](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac/)\\n\\n### S11 \u2014 No wildcard RBAC\\n**Why it matters:** A ClusterRole with `verbs: [\"*\"]`, `resources: [\"*\"]`, or `apiGroups: [\"*\"]` is cluster-admin by another name and bypasses the intent of RBAC.\\n**Steps:** Replace wildcards with explicit verbs/resources the workload actually uses; audit with `kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq` filtering for `\"*\"` (exclude built-in `admin`/`cluster-admin`/`edit`/`system:` roles).\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Identity and Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/identity-and-access-management.html)\\n\\n### S12 \u2014 Access Entries / API auth mode *(AWS-API)*\\n**Why it matters:** The `aws-auth` ConfigMap is deprecated and error-prone; the Cluster Access Management API with Access Entries is the current, auditable standard.\\n**How to verify / fix:** `aws eks describe-cluster --name ${CLUSTER} --query cluster.accessConfig.authenticationMode` (target `API`); migrate principals to Access Entries.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Cluster Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/cluster-access-management.html)\\n\\n### S13 \u2014 IRSA / Pod Identity for workloads\\n**Why it matters:** Workloads using the node IAM role inherit the node\\'s broad permissions. Per-workload identity (EKS Pod Identity, preferred; or IRSA) scopes AWS access to exactly what the pod needs.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Identify workloads making AWS calls via the node role (no SA annotation / Pod Identity association).\\n2. Prefer **EKS Pod Identity** (no OIDC config, supports session tags/ABAC; pre-deployed on Auto Mode); use IRSA where Pod Identity isn\\'t an option.\\n**Snippet (IRSA-annotated ServiceAccount):**\\n```yaml\\napiVersion: v1\\nkind: ServiceAccount\\nmetadata:\\n  name: ${APP}-sa\\n  namespace: ${NAMESPACE}\\n  annotations:\\n    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::${ACCOUNT_ID}:role/${ROLE_NAME}\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Cluster Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/cluster-access-management.html)\\n- [EKS User Guide \u2014 EKS Pod Identities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/pod-identities.html)\\n\\n### S14 \u2014 automountServiceAccountToken disabled where unused\\n**Why it matters:** A mounted SA token a workload doesn\\'t use is a free credential for an attacker who compromises the pod \u2014 it can call the Kubernetes API as that SA.\\n**Steps:** Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the SA or pod for workloads that don\\'t call the API; leave on only where in-cluster API access is needed.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\napiVersion: v1\\nkind: ServiceAccount\\nmetadata: { name: ${APP}-sa, namespace: ${NAMESPACE} }\\nautomountServiceAccountToken: false\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Identity and Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/identity-and-access-management.html)\\n\\n### S15 \u2014 NetworkPolicy default-deny coverage\\n**Why it matters:** By default all pod-to-pod traffic is allowed (flat east/west). A compromised pod can reach everything. VPC CNI Network Policy is **not enabled by default** \u2014 the baseline is default-deny per namespace plus an explicit DNS allow.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Enable Network Policy on the VPC CNI addon (`ENABLE_NETWORK_POLICY=true`) or use a policy-capable CNI.\\n2. Apply a default-deny (ingress+egress) per workload namespace, then a DNS-allow, then incrementally allow required flows.\\n**Snippet (default-deny + DNS allow):**\\n```yaml\\napiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1\\nkind: NetworkPolicy\\nmetadata: { name: default-deny, namespace: ${NAMESPACE} }\\nspec:\\n  podSelector: {}\\n  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]\\n---\\napiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1\\nkind: NetworkPolicy\\nmetadata: { name: allow-dns, namespace: ${NAMESPACE} }\\nspec:\\n  podSelector: {}\\n  policyTypes: [Egress]\\n  egress:\\n    - to:\\n        - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } }\\n          podSelector: { matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns } }\\n      ports: [{ protocol: UDP, port: 53 }, { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }]\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Network Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/network-security.html)\\n- [EKS User Guide \u2014 Configure your cluster for Kubernetes network policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/cni-network-policy.html)\\n'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}, {"id": "tooluse_RdhA4Sk40zPPndRs55WFiM", "content": "[{'text': '# Security Network Nodes remediations \u2014 shard 01\\nCanonical IDs: `S16,S17,S18,S19,S20,S21,S22,S23`\\n\\n### S16 \u2014 No webhook catch-all rules\\n**Why it matters:** An admission webhook matching `apiGroups:[\"*\"]` AND `resources:[\"*\"]` intercepts every API call \u2014 a single point of failure and a latency tax on all operations.\\n**Steps:** Scope webhook `rules` to the specific apiGroups/resources/operations the webhook actually needs.\\n**References:**\\n- [Kubernetes \u2014 Dynamic Admission Control](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/extensible-admission-controllers/)\\n\\n### S17 \u2014 Webhook failurePolicy on system namespaces\\n**Why it matters:** A webhook with `failurePolicy: Fail` that also intercepts kube-system can block control-plane operations if the webhook backend is down \u2014 a cluster-wide outage risk.\\n**Steps:** Exempt kube-system/kube-public via `namespaceSelector`, or set `failurePolicy: Ignore` for non-critical webhooks.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\nnamespaceSelector:\\n  matchExpressions:\\n    - { key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name, operator: NotIn, values: [kube-system, kube-public] }\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [Kubernetes \u2014 Dynamic Admission Control](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/extensible-admission-controllers/)\\n\\n### S18 \u2014 External secrets management\\n**Why it matters:** Raw Kubernetes Secrets are base64 (not encrypted) and live in etcd; sprawl of sensitive data in Secrets widens the blast radius of an etcd or RBAC compromise.\\n**Steps:** Use External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI Driver to source secrets from AWS Secrets Manager / Parameter Store at runtime; pair with KMS envelope encryption (SM1).\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Data encryption and secrets management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/data-encryption-and-secrets-management.html)\\n\\n### S19 \u2014 Secrets via volume not env\\n**Why it matters:** Secrets injected as env vars leak through crash dumps, `/proc`, logging, and `kubectl describe` more readily than mounted files.\\n**Steps:** Mount secrets as files (volume) instead of `env`/`envFrom`; the app reads from the mounted path.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Data encryption and secrets management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/data-encryption-and-secrets-management.html)\\n\\n### S20 \u2014 Image pull policy / no :latest\\n**Why it matters:** `:latest` (or untagged) images are non-deterministic \u2014 two pods can run different code, and rollbacks are impossible. It also defeats image provenance.\\n**Steps:** Pin explicit, immutable tags (or digests); set ECR repositories to `IMMUTABLE`; set `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` with pinned tags.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\ncontainers:\\n  - name: ${APP}\\n    image: ${ACCOUNT}.dkr.ecr.${REGION}.amazonaws.com/${REPO}:1.4.2\\n    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Image Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/image-security.html)\\n\\n### S21 \u2014 Image scanning present\\n**Why it matters:** Unscanned images ship known CVEs into the cluster. Continuous scanning catches them before and after deploy.\\n**Steps:** Enable Amazon ECR enhanced scanning (Inspector) on repositories, or run Trivy/Grype in CI and in-cluster.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Image Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/image-security.html)\\n- [Amazon ECR \u2014 Image scanning](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/image-scanning.html)\\n\\n### S22 \u2014 GuardDuty EKS protection\\n**Why it matters:** GuardDuty EKS Protection (audit-log + runtime monitoring) detects threats like crypto-mining, privilege escalation, and suspicious API calls that static checks miss.\\n**Steps:** Enable GuardDuty EKS Audit Log Monitoring and EKS Runtime Monitoring (agent auto-managed) for the account.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Runtime Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/runtime-security.html)\\n- [GuardDuty \u2014 EKS Protection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/kubernetes-protection.html)\\n\\n### S23 \u2014 Policy enforcement engine\\n**Why it matters:** Pod Security Admission enforces only the built-in PSS levels. ## 4. Detailed findings
All remediations are proposals for human approval. Nothing was changed. "3 workloads" means `default/Deployment/legacy-web`, `team-a/Deployment/env-secret-app` and `team-a/Pod/hostnet-pod`.

**S2 — No host namespaces (High, Regressed)**
- **Evidence:** `team-a/hostnet-pod` has `spec.hostNetwork: true` and podIP 10.42.0.64, equal to the node IP. No hostPID or hostIPC anywhere. Other hostNetwork pods are AWS-managed system pods: aws-node, kube-proxy and the GuardDuty agent.
- **Severity:** High is the baseline. The cluster has 2 nodes and no admission control, so any user can create another pod like it.
- **Impact:** the pod sits in the node's network namespace and can sniff or reach node-local services. The IMDS hop limit of 1 limits IMDS access from normal pod networking, but a host-network pod originates from the node itself. This is general EC2 behavior, not something I tested. S28 stays PASS because the instance settings are correct.
- **Fix:** remove `hostNetwork` (set `hostNetwork: false`, `hostPID: false`, `hostIPC: false`). Enforce with PSA `baseline` or `restricted` on `team-a`.
- **Link:** [EKS Best Practices — Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)

**S3 — allowPrivilegeEscalation=false (High, Persisting)**
- **Evidence:** unset on the 3 workloads. `hardened-app` sets it false.
- **Impact:** a process can gain more privileges than its parent through setuid binaries.
- **Fix:** set `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` on every container and enforce via PSA.
- **Link:** [Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)

**S4 — Drop ALL capabilities (High, Persisting)**
- **Evidence:** no `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` on the 3 workloads.
- **Impact:** containers keep the default capability set.
- **Fix:** drop ALL and add back only what is needed.
- **Link:** [Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)

**S7 — runAsNonRoot (High, Persisting)**
- **Evidence:** `runAsNonRoot` is unset on the 3 workloads. Status shows uid 65535 for the pause image, but nothing enforces it.
- **Impact:** a different image could silently run as root.
- **Fix:** set `runAsNonRoot: true` and a concrete `runAsUser`.
- **Link:** [Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)

**S32 — StorageClass encryption (High, Persisting)**
- **Evidence:** `gp2` has `parameters: {fsType: ext4, type: gp2}` with no `encrypted`.
- **Impact:** any PVC using it provisions an unencrypted EBS volume. No PVs exist yet, so no data is exposed today.
- **Fix:** use `parameters: { type: gp3, encrypted: "true", kmsKeyId: <KMS key ARN> }`. Note that no EBS CSI add-on is installed.
- **Link:** [Data encryption and secrets management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/data-encryption-and-secrets-management.html)

**SM3 — Endpoint exposure (High, Persisting)**
- **Evidence:** `endpointPublicAccess: true`, `publicAccessCidrs: ["0.0.0.0/0"]`, private access also enabled.
- **Severity:** I kept High to match the previous run and the skill's check table. The cluster is non-prod and temporary.
- **Impact:** the API server is reachable from the whole internet.
- **Fix:** restrict `publicAccessCidrs` to known ranges, or go private-only.
- **Link:** [Cluster Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/cluster-access-management.html)

**S5 — seccomp RuntimeDefault (Medium, Persisting)**
- **Evidence:** no seccompProfile on the 3 workloads.
- **Impact:** no syscall filtering.
- **Fix:** set `seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}` at pod level.
- **Link:** [Runtime Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/runtime-security.html)

**S6 — readOnlyRootFilesystem (Medium, Persisting)**
- **Evidence:** unset on the 3 workloads.
- **Impact:** a compromised container can write binaries or config.
- **Fix:** set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` and mount `emptyDir` for the paths that must be writable.
- **Link:** [Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)

**S9 — Pod Security Admission (Medium, Persisting)**
- **Evidence:** `default` and `team-a` have only the `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` label. `secure-ns` enforces `restricted`. System namespaces are excluded from this finding.
- **Impact:** nothing blocks privileged, root or host-namespace pods in `default` and `team-a`. This is how `hostnet-pod` was admitted.
- **Fix:** label with `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline` and `warn: restricted`.
- **Link:** [Enforce Pod Security Standards with Namespace Labels](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/enforce-standards-namespace-labels/)

**S12 — Access Entries / API auth mode (Medium, Persisting)**
- **Evidence:** the authentication mode is `API_AND_CONFIG_MAP`. `aws-auth` exists and maps only the node role `ops-delta-test-NodeRole-…`, which also has an access entry. The cluster has 9 access entries.
- **Impact:** the deprecated ConfigMap is still an active access path.
- **Fix:** keep entries in Access Entries and move to `API` mode after validating nothing depends on `aws-auth`.
- **Link:** [Cluster Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/cluster-access-management.html)

- **Evidence:** the token is auto-mounted (projected `kube-api-access-*` volume) on the 3 workloads, all on the `default` service account. `hardened-app` sets it false.
